Within the spherically symmetric axial ansatz, we characterize Ricci-symmetric affine connections by the condition $(fV-U)'=0$ and compare a constant-$W=fV-U$ family with a constant-$U$ family. Although these connections share the same metric and torsion scalar, their affine curvature invariants generally differ. Independent coordinate-level curvature contractions and component tests of the unrestricted metric and connection variations corroborate the identities used in the construction; these checks complement the analytic variational derivation. Finally, we identify null directions of the restricted axial quadratic form and distinguish this degeneracy from a complete metric-affine stability analysis. Our conclusions are local and do not establish global extendibility, physical inequivalence of all torsion profiles, or dynamical stability.

papers.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?
papers.abstract: A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator. The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.

papers.title: $K_1^*(1870)$ and $3S$-$2D$ mixing in the strange meson sector
papers.abstract: Very recently, the BESIII Collaboration reported the first observation of a $J^P=1^-$ strange resonance in the $Kη'$ system, the $K_1^*(1870)$. We examine whether this state can be accommodated in the kaon meson family. Although it cannot be assigned as a pure $3^3S_1$ or $2^3D_1$ state, we show that it can be described as the lower state of $3S$-$2D$ mixing, whose mass agrees with the measured value, and we predict its higher-mass partner. Using the quark pair creation model, we calculate the OZI-allowed decay properties of both \textcolor{black}{mixed} states; the total decay width of the lower state is consistent with the measured width of the $K_1^*(1870)$. We note that the subordinate $Kη'$ decay mode of this state appears to contradict its observed $Kη'$ decay channel, which calls for further study. We further investigate the production of these two states via the $Kp$ reaction, which may provide valuable information for future experimental searches.

papers.title: Asymptotic Divergence-Based Monitoring for Data Drift in Production AI Systems: A Discrete Case Approach
papers.abstract: We develop a complete asymptotic theory for monitoring data drift in production artificial intelligence (AI) systems whose inputs take values in a finite set of categories. The framework combines two complementary inferential tools. Under the no-drift hypothesis $H_0$, the two-sample likelihood-ratio statistic $G$ of Wilks follows a universal Chi_{r-1}^2 law, independently of the divergence chosen and of the sample sizes; the calibrated Population Stability Index (PSI) of Yurdakul and Naranjo (2021) shares the same Chi_{r-1}^2 limit and is asymptotically equivalent to the $G$-test under $H_0$. Under the drift hypothesis $H_1$, the plug-in phi-divergence is asymptotically normal with a variance computed in closed form for the one-sample, two-sample and symmetrized configurations, yielding standardized $Z$-statistics, detection boundaries, power functions and sample-size planning rules. We supply a per-category decomposition that localizes the drift on specific categories, a Benjamini--Hochberg procedure for monitoring many features simultaneously, and an explicit comparison with the heuristic PSI cut-offs of industrial practice. Two fully worked simulation examples - one one-sample with the Rényi divergence and multiple testing, one two-sample with the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence and sample-size planning - illustrate every notion of the paper on realistic production data.

papers.title: Maximality of the Došen--Petrić Boolean Category
papers.abstract: We prove that the zero-identity Boolean category of Došen and Petrić, freely generated by a nonempty set of propositional variables, is maximal. Adjoining any equation between parallel morphisms that does not follow from the defining equations, and closing under the operations on morphisms and uniform formula substitution, collapses this category to a preorder. This disproves their conjecture that the category is not maximal. The proof uses Boolean Coherence to select a pair of variable occurrences on which the two morphisms differ. Composition with morphisms selecting these occurrences, uniform substitution and two isomorphisms yield equality of the product projections. We prove that any zero-identity Boolean category satisfying such an additional equation under every interpretation of the variables is a preorder. We also give a Lean formalization of these proofs and their dependencies. It includes Boolean Coherence and the correspondence between substitution on tagged occurrence sets and substitution on finite ordinals.

papers.title: Vegetation Health Classification for Low-Data and Edge Hardware Deployment
papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) equipped with cameras are popular, viable tools for vegetation and environmental health monitoring. However, existing image classification methods are incompatible with UAV implementation for independent practitioners in remote, resource-constrained environments due to large dataset requirements, GPU hardware, inflexible retraining, and low interpretability. This paper presents a lightweight, interpretable vegetation classification algorithm operating with as few as five reference images per class, without GPUs or heavy machine learning frameworks. It uses a 2D hue-saturation histogram feature representation and Earth Mover's Distance or Quadratic Form Distance, paired with a log-likelihood probability score, to classify images into three vegetation health categories. We evaluated six systems: three custom pipelines and three established models across low-data scenarios ($n = 5, 10, 25$) and a full-data regime of 2,172 drone images from 28 South American locations. Our custom pipelines achieve competitive Top-1 accuracy (81--85\%) under low-data constraints, maintaining sub-1ms inference times that enable real-time classification and subsequently tasks such as seeding and watering. The algorithms also support incremental retraining without full model reconstruction. We validate edge feasibility by deploying the QFD variant on an ESP32 microcontroller, achieving 82.8\% accuracy with 1.01\% heap memory utilization (45kb), demonstrating that effective vegetation classification is achievable on low-cost, low-power embedded hardware without cellular connectivity.

papers.title: A quantitative measure of predictability for surface gravity waves
papers.abstract: We introduce a Bayesian inference framework to characterize the predictability of a one dimensional ocean surface wave field given surface elevation measurements from a sensor. Unlike the classical theories that only sketch the boundary of a predictable zone based on group velocity, we use the Bayesian posterior uncertainty of surface elevation to quantify the local predictability at every spatiotemporal location. Our approach first constructs a prior distribution to encode existing knowledge of the wave field such as the spectrum and propagation direction. By conditioning on the (possibly noisy) measurement data, we infer the posterior distribution of the wave field, from which a spatiotemporal uncertainty map is extracted. This map agrees well with the group-velocity-based classical predictable zone theory when the frequency spectrum has bounded support. Meanwhile, it also demonstrates predictability even for a spectrum with unbounded frequency support where the classical predictable zone degenerates. A refined analysis of posterior uncertainty using observability Gramian matrix reveals a `data-informed' part and an `un-informed' part of the wave field, with the latter being fundamentally un-predictable. Furthermore, nonlinear effects can be naturally introduced into the Bayesian framework by incorporating the nonlinear ocean surface wave equations. This is the first time that nonlinearity is rigorously treated in the predictable zone problem. We perform numerical tests using both bounded, piecewise constant spectrum and unbounded JONSWAP spectrum. The numerical results confirm the proposed advantages of our method for linear waves and reveal how wave steepness affects the predictability of nonlinear waves. Nonlinear modal interactions redistribute uncertainty between the inside and the outside of the predictable zone with an amount proportional to the wave steepness.

papers.title: Beyond Paired Inputs: Learning to Leverage RGB-T Cross-Modal Relations in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.abstract: RGB and thermal infrared (TIR) sensors provide complementary observations, yet their distinct sensing characteristics make effective cross-modal coordination challenging. Although existing multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process paired RGB-T inputs, they often fail to translate cross-modal relations into effective task-specific decisions, leaving the potential of these relations to improve task performance and robustness largely untapped. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RelMLLM, an RGB-T MLLM that explicitly learns to exploit cross-modal relations in task-specific decision making. It represents modality reliability, the cross-modal relation, and the dominant modality as a verifiable decision state. We derive task-grounded supervision for this state by comparing RGB-only, TIR-only, and paired RGB-T task outcomes. A hierarchical relation-guided reward supervises modality-specific evidence, relation-state prediction, and the final task output, while encouraging consistency across evidence, relation, and decision. We evaluate RelMLLM on natural RGB-T grounding, RGB-T visual question answering, and held-out sensor degradation. RelMLLM improves grounding accuracy and degradation robustness over its Qwen3-VL baselines while preserving performance on general RGB-T reasoning benchmarks. These results demonstrate that effectively exploiting cross-modal relations leads to more accurate and robust RGB-T decisions. Code and model weights are publicly available.

papers.title: Quaternion Matrix Tuples with Common Invariant Subspaces: Dimension and Nonuniqueness
papers.abstract: Let $M_n(\mathbb{H})$ denote the algebra of $n\times n$ quaternion matrices. We study common invariant right subspaces of tuples in $M_n(\mathbb{H})^r$ and determine exact real semialgebraic dimensions for two associated sets. If $n_1,\ldots,n_s$ are positive integers, $n=n_1+\cdots+n_s$, and $q=\sum_{1\leq a<b\leq s}n_an_b$, the set of tuples preserving at least one nested chain with successive increments $n_1,\ldots,n_s$ has dimension $4rn^2-4(r-1)q$. For $r\geq2$ and $1\leq k<n$, the set of tuples with at least two distinct common $k$-dimensional right invariant subspaces has dimension $4rn^2-4(r-1)(k(n-k)+n-1)$. The proofs use finite right-module coordinates and a common local-rank argument.

papers.title: Unbound matter in the circum-halo medium: a common mediator of halo secondary bias
papers.abstract: Halo secondary bias describes the dependence of halo clustering on properties beyond mass. Here we report that a new environmental metric, the unbound matter fraction ($f_{\rm un}$) in the $2$--$3\,R_{\rm vir}$ shell around a halo, can largely account for secondary bias. Using haloes with $M_{\rm vir}=10^{10.5}$--$10^{14.5}h^{-1}{\rm M_\odot}$ at $z=0$ obtained from TNG300-1-Dark, we find that controlling for $f_{\rm un}$ reduces the secondary bias of formation time, concentration, spin, shape and velocity anisotropy to a residual correlation of $\lesssim 4\%$, outperforming other environmental metrics such as the tidal anisotropy for spin and velocity anisotropy. Applying a stacking method to the circum-halo medium (CHM), we identify two distinct flow patterns: low-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes co-move with coherent flows, with the CHM converging onto the haloes; in contrast, high-$f_{\rm un}$ haloes move through dynamically hot, partially virialized structures, with the CHM passing by rather than being accreted. This dichotomy points to two distinct regimes of secondary bias, a `cold' regime and a `hot' regime, in which tidal and inertial forces act as the main drivers, respectively, with the dominant mechanism migrating from the former to the latter as haloes assemble into massive structures. At fixed large-scale environment, $f_{\rm un}$ further indicates the presence of nearby neighbours and the competitive accretion. Our results highlight the role of unbound matter as a mediator of environmental effects on haloes, and reveal the physical mechanisms that shape the CHM pattern through which these effects are mediated.

papers.title: Fixed-space indices and symmetry breaking in variational problems
papers.abstract: We establish a quantitative criterion for variational bifurcation with prescribed exact stabilizers under finite group actions. Combining scalar spectral flow on fixed spaces with overgroup nullities, we bound the number of bifurcation parameters when the restricted singular set is finite. The theorem allows strongly indefinite Fredholm Hessians and singular ambient endpoints, without parameter differentiability or regular crossings. Finite Morse index reduces the inputs to indices and nullities; extensions cover varying form domains and regular matrix Sturm--Liouville systems. For a Newtonian nine-body family containing a reported counterexample to Moeckel's stability conjecture, we prove analytically that two nonconjugate exact reflection types bifurcate at a common central mass, displacing the central body. Positivity excludes larger stabilizers, while a scalar Schur complement synchronizes the bifurcations, independently of the reported stability assertion.

papers.title: Sustaining In-Network Computation in Satellite Networks: An Architecture for Semantic Continuity
papers.abstract: Satellite computations often outlast the paths and providers initially serving them. We argue that in-network computing should organize changing execution opportunities around one continuing logical computation: workers execute ready operations, while consumers recognize which results already contribute. We present an architecture separating logical computation, stream context, and physical binding, and show in wildfire assessment how retained observations support recomputation while reachable association history stays in place. A 300-node Linux prototype examines placement, dependency assembly, and continuation. Across 120 images, stage-wise placement delivers 82.08% of positions within deadlines versus 76.06% for single-node placement, while traces separate blocked output delivery from dependencies split across providers. Across 50 observations with 20-node isolation, Confirmation-Coordinated Rebinding (CCR) coordinates replanning, source replay, cross-attempt acceptance, and in-band confirmation to complete all 50 observations with verified outputs using seven replays and 13 ignored duplicate outputs.

papers.title: Ship-as-a-buoy for Phase-resolved Reconstruction of Surface Waves
papers.abstract: We develop a data assimilation framework to address the ``ship-as-a-buoy'' problem, i.e., estimation of the wave field from time series of ship motion. Unlike previous algorithms which only provide information of wave spectrum, our approach reconstructs the instantaneous phase-resolved wave field. The full framework includes two steps: the first step to generate an initial (rough) estimation of the wave field using the response-amplitude-operators (RAOs), and the second step to refine the reconstruction using an ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to incorporate the measured motion time series. Together with EnKF in the second step, we model the coupled wave-ship dynamics by a high-order spectral (HOS) method for waves and a Cummins equation for ship motion (although higher-fidelity ship model can be applied). We conduct extensive tests of our method for the case with one ship, and the naturally extended cases with multiple ships or with uncertain parameters in the ship motion model. For all test cases we demonstrate favorable reconstruction of the wave field, which in general further improves with the number of ships available and with uncertain parameters properly estimated. We also provide insights on the successful reconstruction in terms of ensemble correlations between the motion time series and features of the wave field.

papers.title: Self-similarity of axisymmetric Marangoni flows on a deep viscous subphase
papers.abstract: Local gradients of surface tension caused by inhomogeneous distributions of surfactant molecules are known to generate Marangoni flows, the mechanics of which have important consequences in various areas of science and engineering. In this paper, we investigate the deposition of insoluble surfactants on the surface of a deep, viscous subphase, which propagate axisymmetrically without diffusing. We study these flows from the perspective of self-similarity, i.e., seeking solutions which show universal features on appropriate length and time scales. We first present a closed form, self-similar solution of the first kind for the axisymmetric spreading of surfactants, which is globally valid at long times. We then numerically study `filling' flows of surfactant, where the surfactant distribution is locally depleted such that inward flows are generated to `fill' the surfactant-free area. These flows have the special feature of forming cusp-like structure in finite time, which have been studied extensively in the literature of self-similarity of the second kind. We show that these flows admit a countably infinite number of stable similarity solutions based on the local behavior of the initial surfactant concentration profile. We remark on a few unique features of these results in contrast to filling flows in other physical limits.

papers.title: Galerkin methods for unconventional superconductors with long-range interactions on 3D lattices
papers.abstract: We develop an analysis and a B-spline Galerkin method for the matrix-valued Bardeen-Cooper-Schrieffer (BCS) gap equation of unconventional superconductors with general long-range interaction kernels on arbitrary Bravais lattices. We define the BCS free energy functional on lattices, show that it is bounded from below, and characterise solutions of the gap equation as its stationary points. For non-repulsive kernels, we prove that fixed-point iteration never increases the free energy and drives the residual to zero. The algebraically decaying tails of the interaction are described by Epstein zeta functions, so the method applies to any power-law exponent $ν>0$, including exponents at or below the lattice dimension such as dipolar interactions in three-dimensional lattices. In the B-spline Galerkin basis, the singular convolutions correspond to block-circulant matrices whose eigenvalues are lattice sums, applied without quadrature at FFT cost. Each iteration takes log-linear work and linear memory, and Broyden updates accelerate convergence. By engineering a suitable dispersion for a prescribed gap, we obtain non-trivial analytic singlet and triplet solutions of the gap equation with power-law interactions on the integer lattice at zero temperature, to our knowledge the first ones. Benchmarks against these solutions and against highly resolved numerical data show convergence rates determined by the B-spline degree and the regularity of the solution. Finally, we compute a nodal superconductor with long-range interactions on the three-dimensional fcc lattice: a chiral state with a line node and two topologically non-trivial Weyl point nodes. On 16 cores, the method reaches a residual of $1.5\times10^{-13}$ for 6.3 million complex unknowns in less than two minutes.

papers.title: PALIN: Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR Multimodal 3D Object Detection with Benchmark
papers.abstract: 3D object detection is critical for intelligent transportation systems. LiDAR has been widely adopted for accurate geometric measurements; however, purely geometric representations remain ambiguous under sparse observations and occlusions, while cross-sensor multimodal fusion suffers from calibration and synchronization errors. To overcome these challenges, we leverage an Ouster LiDAR to construct PALIN (Pixel-Aligned LiDAR-NIR), a large-scale intrinsically pixel-aligned multimodal dataset jointly capturing geometry and NIR intensity, comprising approximately 8,000 annotated frames from static urban intersections and diverse mobile suburban scenes. Building upon this dataset, we propose CMambaFusion, a novel fusion framework consisting of a four-directional Cross-Mamba module for bidirectional cross-modal interaction and a Gated Concat-Mamba module for joint feature refinement. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PALIN enables effective multimodal learning, and CMambaFusion achieves superior accuracy-efficiency trade-offs over both LiDAR-only and representative fusion baselines.

papers.title: Leveraging Dual-Process Theory for Multimodal Multiparty Turn-Taking Prediction
papers.abstract: In multiparty conversations, a pause does not always mean a speaker has finished, and another voice does not necessarily indicate a change in who holds the conversational floor. Reliable turn-taking therefore requires recognising not only whether a speaker is ready to yield the floor, but also when a possible transition deserves attention. We propose a dual-process-inspired framework that separates continuous candidate discovery from selective verification. A fast, recall-oriented stage identifies plausible transition points. In contrast, a deliberative stage combines acoustic, linguistic, speaker-related, and predicted future-activity evidence, together with multimodal cues where available, to reject false candidates and refine transition timing. We evaluate the framework through three distinct tasks: SHIFT/HOLD classification at supplied decision points, verification of automatically generated candidates, and continuous discovery and localisation of floor transfers. On VoxConverse, we derive action-aware turn-taking events from speaker-diarization annotations to examine unconstrained conversations with varying numbers of speakers. Multi-TPC provides complementary evaluation of controlled triadic interactions using speech, gaze, motion, and prosodic information. The findings reveal that identifying plausible transitions is considerably easier than reliably confirming and localising genuine floor transfers, while the contribution of individual evidence sources varies across conversational settings. These results highlight the importance of treating multiparty turn-taking as a continuous discovery-and-verification problem rather than classification at predefined boundaries.

papers.title: Bright-Dark State Interplay Governs Vibronic Decoherence in Molecular Aggregates
papers.abstract: In this study, we establish a spectroscopy-driven framework that connects optically bright vibronic eigenstates to their subsequent decoherence dynamics in excitonic molecular aggregates. Combining the Multiparticle Holstein Formalism with explicit system--bath interactions, we demonstrate that relaxation-induced purity loss is governed by three interconnected factors: (i) the bath spectral window, which determines the accessibility of intra- and interband relaxation pathways; (ii) the local network of dark vibronic states surrounding the optically prepared bright state; and (iii) the energetic placement of the bright state, which controls downhill relaxation. Remarkably, states with different excitation energies exhibit nearly identical purity dynamics when their local relaxation networks are similar. The resulting H--J asymmetry further reveals the importance of energetic directionality. These findings establish a reliable connection between optical spectroscopy, vibronic band structure, and state-selective loss in purity.

papers.title: UACS: Uncertainty-Aware Clustering and Sparse Parameter Estimation for Multi-Condition Wheel Center Force
papers.abstract: Accurate wheel center force (WCF) estimation is important for vehicle durability analysis and condition monitoring, whereas direct measurement requires dedicated transducers and increases instrumentation cost and complexity. As a result, soft sensors have attracted considerable attention as a practical alternative. However, developing reliable soft sensors remains challenging due to varying working conditions, unknown condition relationships, and high-dimensional model representations. This paper proposes an uncertainty-aware clustering and sparse parameter estimation framework (UACS) for WCF signal estimation under diverse and unlabeled working conditions. A MISO-FIR model is first constructed using easily accessible sensor signals to estimate the unmeasurable force signal. The uncertainty of estimated parameters is quantified through confidence ellipsoids, and pairwise hypothesis testing is developed to identify statistically similar working conditions. Based on these uncertainty-aware comparisons, working conditions are grouped in an unsupervised manner, and sparse parameter estimation is performed within each cluster. The UACS framework simultaneously reduces the number of required models and active parameters while maintaining estimation accuracy. Experiments using real-world vehicle data demonstrate that the UACS framework achieves estimation accuracy comparable to condition-specific models while substantially reducing the number of required models and outperforming conventional distance-based clustering approaches.

papers.title: Computing rare events in Lévy-driven systems via optimal control
papers.abstract: We extend the optimal control formulation of sample path large deviation theory, which has proven effective for numerical computation of instantons and sharp probability estimates in stochastic differential equations with Gaussian noise, to systems with light-tailed Lévy noise. In the scaling limit of small jumps and high intensity, such systems satisfy a large deviation principle of Freidlin-Wentzell type, with a running cost given by the Legendre transform of the noise cumulant generating function. We propose to numerically minimize this cost over noise realizations subject to the system dynamics, which yields the instanton without having to solve Hamilton's equations, and naturally handles degenerate and multiplicative noise. When the cumulant generating function has a bounded domain, the cost grows only linearly for large noise, and instantons can contain jumps. We analyze when jumps are not only admissible but optimal, depending on the subleading behavior of the cost and on the drift, and show how jumps can be resolved numerically through a time reparameterization that freezes physical time. For continuous instantons, we derive Riccati and Fredholm determinant expressions for the leading-order prefactor, and we discuss the modifications needed when the instanton jumps. We illustrate and validate our methods against Monte Carlo simulations in several examples: a two-dimensional nonlinear model, an active run-and-tumble particle with non-Gaussian tumbling noise, and the Ghil-Sellers energy balance climate model with Lévy-perturbed solar forcing.

papers.title: Probing SAM Perturbations Through Statistical Replay
papers.abstract: Sharpness Aware Minimization (SAM) updates model parameters using gradients evaluated at adversarially perturbed weights, but it remains unclear which aspects of this procedure are sufficient to reproduce its generalization behavior. In our ResNet 18 experiments on CIFAR 10, simple curvature regularizers based on the Hessian trace and largest eigenvalue remain below SAM in validation accuracy, motivating a direct examination of its perturbations. We introduce statistical replay, a diagnostic that summarizes perturbations from reference SAM trajectories using elementwise means and standard deviations over local windows and constructs new perturbations during independent SGD training. Pure replay uses only these summaries, whereas mixed replay adds isotropic Gaussian noise. Pure replay does not reproduce SAM's validation behavior, while mixed replay and pure isotropic perturbations can approach its validation performance at selected scales without reproducing its training dynamics. An equal radius random direction within SAM performs similarly to SGD, and source, temporal, and layer interventions further suggest that replay behavior depends on perturbation construction. Together, these preliminary results weaken several simple explanations of SAM while leaving an important part of its mechanism unexplained.

papers.title: Local asymptotic normality for Cox-Ingersoll-Ross drift parameters under high-frequency sampling and the strict Feller condition
papers.abstract: For the ergodic Cox--Ingersoll--Ross (CIR) diffusion with known diffusion scale and a fixed initial value, we prove local asymptotic normality (LAN) of the exactly sampled experiment for the drift parameters whenever the Feller index exceeds $1$, assuming only a vanishing mesh and a diverging observation horizon. This improves the previously known condition that the index exceed $(11+\sqrt{89})/2$. The proof cuts off the continuous score near $0$, recovers the remainder by exact conditional centering on each sampling interval, and transfers LAN by a conditional-likelihood argument.

papers.title: Generic finiteness of rotating relative equilibria in the planar $N$-vortex problem
papers.abstract: For every $N\ge2$, we prove that Zariski-generic nonzero real circulations, with any prescribed signs, admit at most $N^{2N}$ labeled, collision-free rotating relative equilibria modulo translations, rotations in $SO(2)$, and positive scaling. The excluded parameters lie in an explicit finite union of quadratic hypersurfaces. The proof combines a logarithmic-residue obstruction to positive-dimensional complex solution sets with Bézout degree bounds.

papers.title: Grokking Can Be Steered: Selecting Desirable Solutions By Choice Of Learning Rule
papers.abstract: During grokking, a network transitions from memorization to generalization, yet what shapes the neural implementation (circuit) of the generalizing solution and specifically the number of participating neurons (its size) remains unclear. We find that the learning rule, the combination of credit assignment algorithm and optimizer, controls this: On modular addition, every learning rule we study that groks recovers the same Fourier-based algorithm, yet implemented by circuits that differ in size. Why? A neuron stays in use when its credit is large relative to the non-gradient term of its own update, and this single condition unifies three routes to unused neurons: the coupled weight decay, Adam's $ε$ and the decay of a trainable per-neuron gain. Equalizing the magnitude of credit assigned to each neuron, or scaling each neuron's weight decay by its credit, expands the effective circuit size, measured from the outgoing weights, from 60% to 99% of the layer's neurons at similar training and test accuracy. We vary which neurons share one equalization factor, from the whole layer to individual neurons, and find that the circuit stays concentrated for groups of eight or more and fully distributes only when every neuron has its own factor. Credit magnitudes are usually set by the normalization of standard optimizers: Nero, which normalizes per neuron, distributes the computation, whereas Adam and seven others, including RMSProp, Muon, and Shampoo, use other normalization schemes and retain small, concentrated circuits. Distributed circuits tolerate neuron deletion better, while concentrated circuits can be pruned further and transfer about twice as fast to a task that recombines the same features, largely by recruiting their unused neurons. Learning rule choice thus steers circuit size, trading robustness against compressibility and transfer speed without changing the learned algorithm.

papers.title: Team Stability: Theory and Evidence
papers.abstract: Teams emerge organically when individuals decide on their own their activities and collaborators. I develop and test a theory in which teams form with consent, interactions reflect team composition, and payoffs feature externalities and several forms of congestion. Stability constraints concern group interactions and require each team member to be willing to remain rather than withdraw or pursue a project alone. Empirical analysis of research collaborations among economists at the Federal Reserve Board suggests that: (i.) these constraints help explain observed teams beyond the payoffs to collaboration; (ii.) estimated violations point to large teams of entrants that appear to be assigned; (iii.) a compensatory mechanism mitigates the effects of variation in policy workload, which appears to affect team composition more than total research output; and (iv.) shifting workload toward experienced economists increases entrants' research output and collaboration, at the cost of lower output among experienced economists who compensate for this shift in policy workload with increased interactions with entrants.

papers.title: StyleJudge: A Human-Validated, In-Context-Learning Vision-Language Evaluator for Artistic Style Transfer
papers.abstract: Automatic evaluation of artistic style transfer remains an open problem: existing metrics score an image pair in isolation, without seeing an example of the intended style transformation, and correlate poorly with human judgment. We introduce StyleJudge, a compact vision-language evaluator conditioned on a small set of reference source-to-stylized pairs before scoring a query pair, mirroring how a human rater calibrates to a style before judging a candidate. On a human-annotated benchmark of 878 rated pairs across 12 artistic styles (728 from 10 training/validation styles, 150 from 2 unseen styles), our efficient 0.8B-parameter StyleJudge reaches a Pearson correlation of 0.291 (Spearman 0.325) with human ratings on seen styles and 0.381 on unseen ones. On seen styles, it achieves the highest positive correlation among tested metrics: Gram-matrix style loss and CLIP similarity correlate weakly ($r=0.041$, $r=0.168$), while LPIPS (scored higher when closer to the source) correlates negatively ($r=-0.404$). We achieve this by distilling evaluation knowledge from a 72B-parameter vision-language teacher used only during training, which reaches $r=0.327$, confirming that most of its human alignment survives compact distillation. For training, we build a dataset of source-to-stylized pairs across the 12 styles via LoRA-adapted diffusion, densified with graded intermediate examples from a high-resolution image-morphing pipeline so the evaluator recognizes partial and complete stylization. On two held-out validation styles, StyleJudge reaches 28.2% exact-match agreement with its teacher's structured scores versus 1.1% for the untuned base model, with 67.8% shorter reasoning traces, and scores a pair in 39 s (median) using 2.5 GB of GPU memory on one NVIDIA T4. We release the human-rating benchmark, annotation guideline, SDXL-adapted FreeMorph code, and model weights.

papers.title: Towards Informed Autonomy Design: Understanding the Interplay of Function Characteristics and Autonomy Preferences in Automotive Agents
papers.abstract: Proactive, autonomous interactions receive high interest in the field of intelligent assistants, including the automotive domain. A central challenge, however, is identifying appropriate levels of autonomy for different functions while maintaining user acceptance and trust. This work examines how function characteristics relate to suitable autonomy levels and whether these relationships generalize across functions. We conducted an expert workshop to define autonomy levels and identify relevant function characteristics. We then collected data from 126 participants, who rated 14 in-vehicle functions regarding autonomy preferences and function characteristics, from which we trained machine learning models to predict appropriate autonomy levels. Building on our findings, we developed our prototypical Autonomy Design Assistant that supports designers in making autonomy-related decisions, which we evaluated qualitatively with nine experts. Our results suggest that function characteristics can rank functions by their suitable level of autonomy and thereby guide more informed autonomy design decisions, whereas predictions for individual users remain uncertain.

papers.title: A Proof of The Twin-Star Hypothesis in Dimension Five
papers.abstract: It was recently shown that the question of whether the determinant-like map \(\det^{S^2}\) is unique up to multiplication by a scalar is equivalent to a combinatorial conjecture regarding cycle-free \(d\)-partitions of the complete graph \(K_{2d}\), known as the twin-star hypothesis. This hypothesis asserts that every cycle-free \(d\)-partition of \(K_{2d}\) is weakly equivalent to one that contains a component isomorphic to the twin-star graph \(TS_d\). This hypothesis was previously established for \(d\le4\). In the present paper, we prove it for \(d=5\). Consequently, the associated determinant-like map \(\det^{S^2}\) is unique up to a scalar in dimension \(5\).

papers.title: InvarOrd: Self-Supervised Ordinal Knowledge Distillation with Rank-Invariant Alignment for Label-Efficient Cross-Species Hyperspectral Fish Freshness Assessment
papers.abstract: Hyperspectral models of fish freshness rarely transfer between species, and labelling a new species is slow and destructive. Freshness is also ordinal, and standard domain alignment can erase that order. We present InvarOrd, which adapts to a new species from 30 labelled cubes (5 per rank) in three stages: self-supervised spectral pretraining on unlabelled source cubes, cross-species alignment by a shrinkage covariance discrepancy computed only within matched ranks, and ordinal distillation into a compact student. The alignment term is provably invariant to the rank means, so it gives no incentive to collapse the ordinal axis. On paired salmon and cod data (800 cubes each, 16 days), a source-trained teacher reaches 1.6 to 1.9 days mean absolute error (MAE) on the other species, with quadratic weighted kappa (QWK) below zero. The 423K-parameter student, 2.54 times smaller than its teacher, attains the lowest MAE (1.476 days) and highest within 1-day accuracy (56.1%) among 14 configurations, matching the best of six ImageNet-pretrained backbones (ConvNeXt-T, 1.503 days) at 66 times fewer parameters, 1.44ms per cube on a GPU and 5s re-adaptation. InvarOrd beats target-only training by 0.29 days (p = 0.031). Among alignment objectives, rank-invariant alignment retains the most ordinal structure (embedding rank correlation 0.183, QWK 0.112), whereas global discrepancy lowers the rank correlation to 0.049 and QWK to zero at only 0.014 days higher MAE.

papers.title: Interpreting Random Forests: Comparing Surrogate Models and Rule Extraction Methods
papers.abstract: Random forests (RFs) often achieve high prediction performance, but their ensemble structure can be difficult to interpret. Surrogate models and rule extraction methods offer interpretable approximations, yet guidance on selecting an appropriate method for a specific research question remains limited. We compared 12 methods for interpreting RFs, with a decision tree as a prediction-oriented reference, across 11 simulation settings and 67 benchmark datasets for regression and classification. Evaluation addressed prediction and structural similarity to the RF, model complexity, prediction performance, and runtime. Simulations additionally assessed explainability using known effect and noise variables. No method performed best across all objectives. For regression, SLIM provided the strongest general performance for prediction similarity or performance on test data, while a linear model offered a simpler global interpretation of linear effects when performance was comparable. For classification, inTrees achieved the strongest overall benchmark performance, with CTree and OC-CART providing useful alternatives. ART consistently produced the most compact representations. NH and SIRUS offered strong structural similarity for regression, while MRT most closely reproduced RF variable usage in the classification simulations, illustrating that prediction-oriented rankings do not necessarily identify the best structural explanation. Outcome-type restrictions, runtime limits, and method-specific failures reduced result availability for several approaches and should be considered alongside performance when selecting a method. Method selection should therefore be guided by the outcome type, anticipated data structure, and intended interpretability objective. Prediction similarity alone is insufficient for explaining an RF and should be considered jointly with structural similarity and model complexity.

papers.title: A Universal Algebraic Construction of Hilbert-Space Fragmentation
papers.abstract: We present a mechanism for obtaining Hilbert-space fragmentation from arbitrary quantum lattice Hamiltonians acting on finite-dimensional local spaces. We first express the Hamiltonian in an algebraic form using supersymmetry (SUSY) and parasupersymmetry (paraSUSY) generators. Enlarging their representations defines a lifting procedure, which we study in two forms, site-wise and bond-wise lifting. Site-wise lifting introduces immobile zero modes that generate exponentially many invariant sectors while retaining the original dynamics in the fully active sector. We determine the sector structure and establish strong fragmentation for uniform lifts at fixed intermediate zero-mode density. For nearest-neighbor chains, correlation functions reveal restricted propagation and, in the mixed-field example, persistent local memory. Bond-wise lifting produces mobile conserved strings, pair-flip dynamics and fluctuating dimers, and extends to fragmented unitary circuits. Different representations and embeddings realize different fragmentation mechanisms. Some of the fragmented models obtained by this method include lifted permutation and Ising spin chains, a lifted toric code, the \(XXC\) families of spin chains, and fragmented extensions derived from the integrable \(H_{1,11}\) and \(H_{1,3}\) seed densities. The last two models are derived from Hietarinta's classification of constant $4\times 4$ Yang-Baxter solutions.

papers.title: Representing Differential Inclusions as Monads: A Framework for Compositional Controller Synthesis
papers.abstract: Sequential composition of safety-certified controllers for hybrid and non-smooth robotic systems is well studied piecewise. Yet no existing framework reduces this question to a single algebraic condition. We construct a \emph{trajectory monad} for Filippov-regular differential inclusions. Its Kleisli category treats controllers as morphisms and sequential execution as trajectory concatenation. Control Barrier Function (CBF) certification, a guarantee of forward invariance, corresponds to a sub-monad of this category. Joint safety of composed controllers then follows from one algebraic condition. All controllers must land in a common sub-monad, which is closed under the monad multiplication. The sub-monad condition recasts recasts existing CBF composition practice categorically. It explains why a smooth intersection of multiple barriers supports safe composition, while enforcing barriers phase by phase does not. For the phase-by-phase case, we derive a closed-form Bernoulli model of the failure rate. We validate it over a randomized sweep of 3{,}000 instances. The same sweep shows that the standard baseline degrades under constraint conflict as the barrier count grows. This baseline enforces all barriers simultaneously as constraints in a single quadratic program (QP). We instantiate the framework on a four-mode piecewise-affine system and on a unicycle reduced-order model over heterogeneous terrain.

papers.title: Deep Nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction for Discretely Observed Functional Data
papers.abstract: We develop a modular framework for deep nonlinear Sufficient Dimension Reduction (SDR) of discretely observed functional predictors with Euclidean or metric-space-valued responses. A presmoothing encoder converts the functional input into finite-dimensional coordinates, and a neural network learns a sufficient representation from them. The framework separates the choice of encoder from that of the SDR criterion. We study kernel embedding and discrete functional principal component analysis, each combined with either a generalized martingale difference divergence network or a Fréchet cumulative covariance network. These combinations share objectives of the martingale difference divergence form. {Under input smoothness and general Hölder regularity of the target operator, we establish approximation and generalization bounds that jointly account for functional truncation, network approximation, statistical estimation, numerical integration, measurement noise, and encoder estimation. The complete theoretical analysis rigorously demonstrates how errors in the encoded coordinates propagate through the network to the deep nonlinear SDR estimator, and quantifies the final estimation error in relation to observation frequency and model complexity.} Simulations and an application to satellite-derived vegetation trajectories and crop-composition responses illustrate the statistical and computational advantages over RKHS-based nonlinear functional SDR methods.

papers.title: Link Spectra of Lorenz-like Templates and the Horseshoe
papers.abstract: We give a complete classification of the inclusion relations between the link spectrum of the horseshoe template $L(0,1)$ and those of the nonnegative Lorenz-like templates $L(0,a)$. For a template $T$, its link spectrum $\mathscr L(T)$ consists of the link types carried by $T$, allowing parallel strands along its strips. For integers $a\geq0$, the spectra of $L(0,a)$ and $L(0,1)$ are comparable under inclusion if and only if $a\notin\{0,2\}$. More precisely, \[ \mathscr L(L(0,a))=\mathscr L(L(0,1)) \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a=1, \] while \[ L(0,a)\prec L(0,1) \qquad (a\geq3). \] For $a=0$ and $a=2$, the two spectra are incomparable. The main new containment is \[ L(0,2n)\preceq L(0,1)\qquad(n\geq2), \] which goes beyond the classical parity-preserving nesting relations. A key ingredient is a braid-theoretic criterion: every $T$-link \[ T((r_1,s_1),\ldots,(r_k,s_k)) \] with $s_k\geq2r_k$ is a horseshoe link. This gives a large explicit family belonging to both the Lorenz and horseshoe spectra. In the reverse direction, we construct a horseshoe link outside the Lorenz spectrum. For each integer $m\geq6$, we obtain infinitely many horseshoe links of braid index $m$ excluded from every other nonnegative $L(0,a)$. These examples give infinitely many links with any prescribed number of components at least three. In the other direction, for each positive number of components, we give infinitely many links carried by both $L(0,0)$ and $L(0,2)$ and excluded from the horseshoe spectrum.

papers.title: Successive Convexification in Learned World Models for Safe Offline Planning
papers.abstract: World models learned from offline data allow an agent to plan without further interaction with the environment, but the sampling-based planners used with them handle safety constraints only by scoring or rejecting sampled action sequences. We instead pose safe planning in the latent space of a learned world model as a successive convex program (SCP), in which a learned discrete-time control barrier function is imposed as a constraint at every step of the horizon. SCP requires smooth dynamics, so we build the networks from smoothed MaxMin activations and spectrally normalised layers, and bound the resulting linearisation error in terms of the Lipschitz bound and the smoothing width. As SCP is a local method, we start it from a sampled plan. On two Safety-Gymnasium navigation tasks with offline data, this planner has fewer violations than MPPI and CEM drawing 128 times as many samples at equal wall-clock time in our main comparison, though not significantly, and earns greater return at longer horizons, and is much safer than SCP without a sampled start. SCP converged more often on Lipschitz-bounded models. Unlike sampling, it also reports at each step whether its plan is a feasible, first-order optimal KKT point of the planning problem in the model, or that no feasible plan was found nearby. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/youngers2006/scwm.

papers.title: VAST: Compiling Grounded Vulnerability Scenarios into Verifiable, Multi-Step Environments for Evaluating LLM Red-Team Agents
papers.abstract: Evaluating Large Language Model (LLM) security agents requires reproducible environments whose workflow difficulty can be varied and whose failures can be diagnosed. We present VAST (Verifiable Adversarial Scenario Training & Evaluation), a declarative range compiler separating vulnerability scenarios from a compiler-introduced workflow-hardening layer. Following a post-hoc code and AST audit across all topics, the main benchmark retains 109 seed edges (45 with strict upstream CVE annotations), 72 family identifiers (62 under shared-HMAC relay grouping), 81 topic configurations (76 core plus 5 bounded execution models), and 1,387 instances (359 canonical four-gate-revalidated specs plus 1,028 seed variants) in a 42:39 partition. On the TopicServer compiler stratum, a budget-matched 270-episode prompt contrast across 10 compiled mechanism-family clusters (30 P2/P3/P4 instances, 40 turns, temperature 0.0) shows that glm-5.3, grok-4.7, and deepseek-v4-pro solve 12/90 instances under contract_only and 14/90 under generic_hint (cluster sign p=1.00), whereas supplying the shared workflow protocol in full_guide lifts completion to 76/90 (28/30, 23/30, 25/30; cluster sign p<=0.00391). On the separate ranges_v2 ledger, a 126-episode evaluation across 6 non-TopicServer workflows and multi-container Docker/Linux stacks solves 88/126 (69.8%) (28/42, 31/42, 29/42), while an 18-episode intervention on asynchronous Redis worker chaining (v2_02) lifts solves from 0/18 to 18/18 (100%) in 4-6 turns when installed worker modules are disclosed in GET /sched/directory. Finally, a three-seed (s in {42, 1024, 2025}) LoRA recipe comparison on Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct across 37 lineage-disjoint families (231 episodes on 33 held-out instances) yields 0/33 for Base, 1.67 +/- 2.89 / 33 for Golden SFT, and 4.67 +/- 2.31 / 33 for Header-Recovery SFT, with all solves on v2_03.

papers.title: The Goldstone--Wilczek Charge on the Rim
papers.abstract: A solenoid flux $Φ=2πα$ threaded through the center of the Kaplan--Sen lattice disk binds a ground-state charge $Q_{\rm core}=α-\mathrm{round}(α)$, and the edge carries exactly the opposite charge. The edge charge is the Goldstone--Wilczek charge of the edge ladder, $Q_{\rm edge}=-\tfrac12η$, with $η$ its spectral asymmetry. At $Φ=π$ one unit of charge crosses the disk. We ask how the rim operator, the Schur complement of the disk Hamiltonian on its boundary sites, registers this transfer. Its count of negative eigenvalues never changes over the flux cycle. Instead, the unit of charge enters the rim through a simple pole: the extremal eigenvalue of the rim operator passes through infinity in the same flux interval as the charge jump, with $ΔQ_{\rm edge}=\tfrac12Δ\,\mathrm{sign}\,λ_{\rm ext}$. The residue factorizes into the coupling of the inner edge mode to the rim and the inverse slope of that mode's level, and grows linearly with the radius. All statements are checked numerically on disks of radius $R=11$, $19$ and $34$.

papers.title: Semantics First, Pixels Later: Mission-Driven Event Streams for Drone Video over Bandwidth-Starved Links
papers.abstract: A surveillance drone on a bandwidth-starved link cannot send the video its operator would need, yet the operator's questions are often not about pixels: did three people converge, when, and where? We study what should cross a link of 1 Mbps down to 1 kbps instead, and in what order. BPS, a behavior-primitive stream, sends semantics first and pixels later: it runs a detector and a tracker onboard and sends short records (25 bytes on average) of multi-frame events selected by a mission card of 16-125 bytes, ahead of positions and pictures. We measure it by what a ground-side language model answers from it, under a preregistered protocol with a held-out set, against H.265 read by the vision fine-tune of the same model, H.265 on which the ground runs our own perception, a stream of quantized tracks, and onboard captions. On the development set (84% of questions about convergence, mostly one location) the event stream answers 74.3% of questions at 0.13 kbps. A reader that receives nothing answers 57.4%, and the video reader 59.6% at 100 kbps and 64.7% on the source frames. When the ground instead runs our perception on the video, video matches the stream at 100 kbps, about 800 times the stream's rate, and falls behind at 64 kbps and below. A track stream matches it at 96 times the bytes and loses 0.03 at 17 times. On held-out data the result is weaker: with events taken from annotated tracks, an oracle, the stream beats H.265 at 100 kbps (+0.13), but with onboard perception it does not (+0.01 [-0.04, +0.06]) and is no better than receiving nothing. Sent alone through emulated links the event records answer 0.739 at 1 Mbps and still 0.724 at 0.3 kbps; an every-frame track stream holds down to 1 kbps and video with ground-side perception down to about 100 kbps. On a Jetson Orin Nano the unchanged pipeline runs at 4.5 fps and misses most events.

papers.title: Rigidity of complete self-shrinkers
papers.abstract: Let $X:M^n\to\R^{n+1}$ be an $n$-dimensional complete self-shrinker with constant squared norm $S$ of the second fundamental form. For $n=4$, we prove that if $f_3=\sum_iλ_i^3$ is constant, where $λ_i$ denotes principal curvatures, then $S=0$, or $S=1$ and the image $X(M^n)$ in the rigid cases is one of the hyperplane, the sphere or the standard generalized cylinders. In every dimension, under assumption of sub-exponential growth we prove the same conclusion. Without assumption of sub-exponential growth, we prove if $S\leq 3+1/\sqrt n$, then the same conclusion holds.

papers.title: Program Distillation: Transferring LLM Capability from System 2 to System 0
papers.abstract: Recent studies leverage large language models (LLMs) to construct executable programs through environment interaction, feedback analysis, and code revision. However, prior work has mainly treated LLMs as optimizers, overlooking their ability to transfer knowledge across system levels. We propose Program Distillation (PD), a framework that formalizes the transfer of abilities from System 2 to System 0. During learning, the LLM provides task knowledge and draft strategies; at deployment, a student program executes the resulting policy. We show that this approach can improve performance while reducing inference time. We introduce PDBench, a benchmark comprising 27 discrete- and continuous-control tasks with fixed initial policies, and PDMetaHarness, a model-harness-independent meta-system for monitoring and guiding the learning process. The strongest model achieves a normalized mean score of 0.728, surpassing PPO (0.656) and Jev-like decision models (0.239), while running exclusively on CPUs and reducing inference costs. Our analysis shows that performance is largely driven by the first breakthrough during learning, and structural modifications have a slightly lower success rate than parameter modifications but typically yield larger gains. We further introduce style distillation, which enables interpretable stylistic control over the learning process. Overall, we present an analytical framework for PD and demonstrate its practical viability.

papers.title: Fluctuation modes in the initial state of heavy-ion collisions: from 2D to 3D hybrid simulations
papers.abstract: This dissertation investigates how the initial stages of relativistic heavy-ion collisions shape the evolution of the quark-gluon plasma (QGP) and the observables measured experimentally. Particular attention is given to the initial state and pre-equilibrium dynamics, which constitute the main sources of uncertainty in hybrid simulations. The first part of the dissertation reviews the framework underlying state-of-the-art hybrid simulations and the numerical tools used in phenomenological analyses. The second part studies the matching between pre-equilibrium evolution and viscous hydrodynamics. Since commonly used conformal kinetic-theory descriptions are inconsistent with the non-conformal hydrodynamic equation of state, an entropy-density matching prescription is proposed. This prescription reduces the artificial bulk pressure generated at the switching time and improves the consistency of the hybrid framework. The third part develops a mode-by-mode decomposition of initial energy-density profiles to isolate fluctuation modes and quantify their contributions to final observables. Applied to Pb-Pb collisions across centrality classes and extended to a fully three-dimensional O-O collision system, the method shows that initial fluctuations survive hydrodynamic evolution and leave measurable imprints on final observables. In O-O collisions, fluctuations can dominate over geometric effects from the impact parameter, demonstrating that intermediate-sized systems are not simply scaled-down versions of large systems. Overall, these results provide tools for constraining the early stages of heavy-ion collisions and for understanding how fluctuations propagate through the QGP evolution.

papers.title: An $(\infty,1)$-category of conically smooth stratified bordisms
papers.abstract: To study derived defect topological quantum field theories, we construct an $(\infty,1)$-category of stratified bordisms and sketch its $(\infty,d)$-dimensional analogue. In the first chapters we develop a method for constructing symmetric monoidal $(\infty,1)$-categories, inspired by Segal spaces but better suited to geometric inputs, which we call interval Segal spaces. Using this framework, we construct the $(\infty,1)$-category of $d$-dimensional smooth manifolds via smooth $\infty$-sheaves thereof, in an attempt to address fibrancy issues present in prior work on this subject. We further equip this category with a symmetric monoidal structure, compute its homotopy 1-category, and extend the construction to manifolds endowed with tangential structures, obtaining the interval Segal space of $d$-dimensional bordisms with tangential structure. To model the stratifications supporting topological defects, we work with conically smooth stratified spaces, a suitably smooth framework for conical stratifications. We define stratified topological manifolds as stratified $\mathcal{B}$-manifolds for a suitable $(\infty,1)$-category of basics $\mathcal{B}$. Using these, we construct an interval Segal space whose objects are compact closed stratified topological $(d-1)$-manifolds and whose 1-morphisms are stratified $d$-dimensional bordisms, and we endow it with a symmetric monoidal structure. We also use tangential structures on conically smooth stratified spaces to formulate a notion of defect labels, aiming toward bordisms with labeled defects in the style of Carqueville et al. Finally, we sketch a higher-dimensional generalization of the interval category to a category of $d$-cubes for $d>1$, conjecturally presenting $(\infty,d)$-categories, and outline how stratified factorization homology may be used to produce derived stratified defect TQFTs.

papers.title: A full-wave ICRH solver with full kinetic accuracy using only first order differential equations
papers.abstract: Accurate full-wave computation of ion cyclotron resonance heating (ICRH) typically requires solving the computationally demanding integro-differential dielectric tensor of the hot plasma. Based on the method in [Phys. Plasmas 32, 082110 (2025)], we develop BO-FW1D, a 1D frequency domain finite difference full-wave solver which generates full kinetic, accurate and efficient simulations utilizing a fluid plasma model. To accurately convert the conductivity tensor in phase space into a first-order differential equation, we introduce a mathematically rigorous framework using pseudodifferential operator theory based on Kohn-Nirenberg ordering. Benchmarks with an all-orders 1D full-wave solver show high consistency in critical kinetic effects and electric-field distributions, while substantial computational acceleration is achieved. This work could lay the foundation for developing full-wave solvers that combine full kinetic accuracy with high computational efficiency.

papers.title: Predicting, Fast and Slow: SSD Already Knows Which Guess Is Wrong
papers.abstract: Heimdall, a learned controller, calls slow on 52% of an SSD's reads when 30% are slow. Uncertainty estimators, the remedy prescribed for its wrong guesses, cannot find them: nine of them do no better than a coin. The drive can. On one trace, 2% of the reads of 4 to 8 KiB that found less than 4 KiB outstanding while the drive was answering came back slow, and Heimdall called 96% of them slow. A 4,096-entry table of how the drive's recent reads came back, untrained and 21 ns a decision, ranks the wrong guesses at a median AUROC of 0.68 on 57 held-out traces, where the nine sit at 0.46 to 0.52, and it predicts slow reads better than Heimdall itself.

papers.title: Characterization of an Optical Time Projection Chamber prototype with Ar:CF$_4$ at atmospheric pressure
papers.abstract: We report on the characterization of an Optical Time Projection Chamber (OTPC) developed as a prototype for neutron-induced reaction studies at Soreq Applied Research Accelerator Facility (SARAF). The prototype was operated with Ar:CF$_4$ (95:5) at 1 bar, using parallel mesh electrodes for charge multiplication and electroluminescence, and alpha particles from a $^{241}$Am source. Both induced charge and light signals were recorded. A systematic characterization was carried out to study charge multiplication and scintillation yield. We present the results of these measurements in single-gap amplification configurations, along with two-gap operation and a demonstration of synchronized optical readout.

papers.title: Text Speeding Itself Up: Recency and Restraint in Session-Local Drafting
papers.abstract: Speculative decoding lets a cheap draft model propose tokens that a large language model verifies in a single forward pass. When the verifier keeps a KV cache, verification is cheap and drafting must be nearly free. Session-local drafters, which predict from the prompt and the text generated so far, meet that bar without training. We compare a recency-weighted, backing-off, confidence-gated session memory against prompt lookup decoding in its reference form, which copies from the earliest earlier match, and in a variant that copies from the most recent one, with paired per-prompt bootstrap intervals throughout. On general, medical, and legal text with a Mistral-7B verifier, recency accounts for the speed: most-recent lookup gains up to 0.09 in speedup over earliest-match lookup on 500-token generations, and session memory's weighting and backoff add nothing measurable on top, at 30 to 40 times the drafting cost. Energy tells a different story. On medical and legal text, unselective drafters are 14% faster than plain decoding yet use as much energy per token, while drafters that abstain on weak evidence save 3 to 4 joules per 100 tokens; a three-token minimum match length on prompt lookup matches the confidence-gated session memory. Outputs are token-identical to greedy decoding in 94% of generations, with every divergence at a numerical near-tie. Under a repetition penalty, long-generation speedups shrink from 1.4-1.7x to 1.1-1.2x, but recency still helps and the length floor is the only drafter that saves energy in both domains.

papers.title: Critical corner angles and defect exchange in confined nematics with splay-bend anisotropy
papers.abstract: In confined nematics, the director turning imposed by the walls is absorbed by defects, and we show that the corners exchange these defects with the liquid. A tangentially anchored corner of opening angle $ω$ takes one of several types, labelled by the number $m$ of half-turns of the director relative to the radius; neighbouring types differ by a bound defect of index $\pm\frac12$, and logarithmic energies decide when the corner sheds or absorbs it. For equal elastic constants the critical angles are $72^\circ$, $120^\circ$, $216^\circ$ and $360^\circ$, with windows of bistability between them, explaining the hidden defect near $72^\circ$ vertices and selecting the equilibria of polygons and discs. We introduce unequal splay and bend constants through the cubic invariant $Q_{lk}\,\partial_lQ_{ij}\,\partial_kQ_{ij}$ in reduced Landau--de Gennes theory; bounding the order by its bulk value makes the problem well posed, without further elastic terms, whenever both Frank constants are positive. At first order only the splay corner feels the anisotropy; other corner and defect energies are even in it and follow exactly by quadrature. The anisotropy moves the angle above which a splay corner sheds a $+\frac12$ defect from $104^\circ$ to $136^\circ$ as $K_3/K_1$ rises from $0.54$ to $1.86$, and so predicts which polygons prefer splay corners and which interior defects. Finite-element computations for polygons of three to eight sides and the disc confirm this: the exchange occurs within the predicted range by migration of $+\frac12$ defects into the corners, near which states with zero, one and two splay corners are nearly degenerate.

papers.title: A Quantum Metric Approach to Stabilizer Codes
papers.abstract: We associate a spectral triple with each stabilizer code in a projective error model arising from a nice error basis and equipped with a length function. The spectral triple records the dimension of the code as well as the minimum code distance. For Pauli stabilizer codes of dimension greater than one with Hamming weight, Latrémolière's dual propinquity provides a pseudometric which allows us to compare codes of different physical and logical dimensions. We show that in the resulting topology, minimum distance of a code is locally constant for qubits and for qudits of dimensions three and five. Thus correction of all errors up to a prescribed weight is a local property in these cases. Moreover, for each prime $p$, we classify the underlying $C^*$-algebras in the metric closure as a subclass of AF algebras, namely those arising as tensor products of $C((\mathbb{Z}_p)^r)$, for $r \in \{0,1,2, \ldots , \infty\}$, with matrix algebras of $p$-power order or the UHF algebra of type $p^\infty$. Every such $C^*$-algebra not isomorphic to $M_{p^k}(\mathbb{C})$ for any $k\geq 1$ occurs as the underlying algebra of a point in the metric boundary. In particular, we obtain the CAR algebra as a metric limit of qubit stabilizer codes.

papers.title: Time-Varying Recalibration of Forecast Distributions
papers.abstract: Combined density forecasts are often miscalibrated, and the miscalibration can change over time. We propose a time-varying framework that recalibrates any combined forecast through applying a monotone map to its probability integral transform. We consider a Beta CDF or a rational quadratic spline as the map, and their parameters are updated either via score-driven filters combined with dynamic model averaging, or by a convolution-based update that additionally conditions on features of the forecast distribution. In simulations, the spline map corrects multimodal miscalibration that the Beta map cannot, and the convolution update achieves the highest log score when the miscalibration switches between regimes. We apply the method to nine G10 exchange rates and US inflation, recalibrating forecast distributions from both a loss-discounting linear pool and Bayesian predictive synthesis. In both applications, recalibration improves PIT uniformity, with gains in forecast accuracy most evident when the original forecasts are miscalibrated.

papers.title: Efficient and Accurate Causal Validation of Training Data Attribution
papers.abstract: Causal validation of training data attribution (TDA) methods is costly, since evaluation involves retraining a model on many different subsets of the original training set. For example, the Linear Datamodeling Score (LDS), which has become a standard metric for evaluating TDA methods, measures the correlation between TDA predictions and expected retrained model outputs. In this paper, we reduce the amount of computation needed to estimate the LDS along three axes: the number of sampled training subsets, the number of retraining seeds per subset, and the number of models in the attribution ensemble. Each of these factors induces a form of bias in the LDS estimation, and removing these sources of bias significantly reduces the number of retrainings needed to match the same accuracy in LDS estimation. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, finite-subset debiasing achieves $3.2\%$ relative RMSE with as few as $4$ subsets, and $32$ subsets match the accuracy of ordinary Spearman using $96$ subsets, measured against a 300-subset reference. On ResNet-9/CIFAR-10, BERT/QNLI and GPT-2/WikiText-2, estimating the training-noise variance allows us to reproduce the standard five-seed LDS at the same accuracy with $2$--$5\times$ fewer retrainings.

papers.title: Counting real meromorphic differentials on $\mathbb{CP}^1$
papers.abstract: The counting problem for meromorphic differentials on $\mathbb{CP}^1$ with fixed orders of zeros and poles and vanishing residues at some specific poles, up to the action of $\mathrm{PGL}_2(\mathbb{C})$ and the multiplication by a nonzero constant, was completely solved before by several authors. In all the cases when there are finitely many such meromorphic differentials, an explicit formula for their number was found and also, in the case of residueless meromorphic differentials with two zeros, a link to the WDVV equations and the KP hierarchy was established. We consider a real analog of these counting problems by requiring that a meromorphic differential is preserved by a real structure on $\mathbb{CP}^1$. Our real counting problems admit refinements, obtained for example by specifying the orders of poles and zeros that are fixed by the antiholomorphic involution. We obtain explicit formulas for all our real counting problems and also, in the case of real meromorphic differentials with two complex conjugate zeros and residueless poles, establish a link to the open WDVV equations and the system of equations for the wave function of the KP hierarchy. An application to real Hurwitz numbers is also presented.

papers.title: Cotorsion pairs in $η$-extensions with applications to $θ$-extension rings and tensor rings
papers.abstract: Let $\mathcal B$ be an abelian category with enough projective and injective objects, and let $\mathcal B\ltimes_ηF$ be an $η$-extension of $\mathcal B$ with $η$ associative. Given a cotorsion pair $(\mathcal X, \mathcal Y)$ in $\mathcal B$, we show that the cotorsion pair $(Δ(\mathcal X),Δ(\mathcal X)^\perp)$ exists for arbitrary associative $η$, removing the square-zero assumption $F^2=0$ from Hu's construction. When $(\mathcal X, \mathcal Y)$ is hereditary, the heredity of $(Δ(\mathcal X),Δ(\mathcal X)^\perp)$ is characterized by the first left derived functor of a canonical defect functor $δ$. We also remark that Hu's construction and hereditary result for the cotorsion pair $({}^\perp U^{-1}(\mathcal Y), U^{-1}(\mathcal Y))$ remain valid without the nilpotence assumption on $η$. Under nilpotence hypotheses, we establish a completeness criterion for $(Δ(\mathcal X),Δ(\mathcal X)^\perp)$ using the Beligiannis radical functor $\mathfrak r$. And we also provide a completeness criterion for $({}^\perp U^{-1}(\mathcal Y), U^{-1}(\mathcal Y))$ if $\mathcal B\ltimes_ηF$ has enough injective objects. We give sufficient conditions for their coincidence. Dual results are obtained for $ζ$-coextensions. Finally, we specialize the theory to $θ$-extension rings and tensor rings, where the abstract conditions admit explicit module-theoretic descriptions.

papers.title: CLEW: Log-Anchored Backward Tracing for Root-Cause Code Localization
papers.abstract: Failures in industrial software systems may involve multiple components and be difficult to reproduce outside the production environment. Root-cause code localization therefore often relies on issue descriptions and runtime logs. However, log evidence may be noisy or incomplete, and the code reporting a symptom may differ from the code containing the underlying defect. These conditions make it challenging to identify relevant log evidence and determine which functions could have caused the reported failure. To address this gap, we introduce CLEW, an agentic approach that combines rule-based log-to-code anchoring with LLM-guided backward code tracing. CLEW organizes selected observations into diagnostic states, guides source exploration from anchored symptom functions, and returns ranked candidate functions, an affected module, and an explanation comprising a proposed mechanism path and associated log events. For evaluation, we construct LogLoc, a benchmark comprising 192 real-world issue and fault-injection cases. Against three baselines, CLEW records the highest observed Acc@1 (77.3%) and MRR (81.3%) on LogLoc-Issues and matches the leading baselines at 97.6% Acc@1 on LogLoc-Airflow. Averaged over all 192 cases, CLEW's wall-clock time is approximately 73% lower than LocAgent's at a similar average inference cost. No aggregate degradation is observed under the tested perturbations, with modest changes in Acc@1 and MRR across the evaluated seeds and base models. These results suggest that CLEW can combine function-level localization with evidence links and runtime efficiency under the evaluated conditions.

papers.title: Cogirth-Strength Ratios and Matroid Rank Reduction
papers.abstract: In the rank-$p$ reduction problem, we are given a matroid with nonnegative element weights and seek a minimum-weight set of elements whose deletion lowers the rank by at least $p$. For graphic matroids, this is the minimum $(p+1)$-cut problem. Chekuri, Quanrud, and Xu developed a tree-packing algorithm for minimum $k$-cut, which relies on the fact that the minimum cut of a graph is at most twice its strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of spanning trees. We generalize this approach from graphs to matroids. The matroid analogue of the minimum cut is the cogirth, the minimum weight of a cocircuit, and the analogue of graph strength is matroid strength, the value of a maximum fractional packing of bases. We show that if every matroid in a deletion-closed class has cogirth at most $d$ times its strength, then for every $p$, the natural linear programming relaxation of rank-$p$ reduction is within a factor of $d$ of the optimum. As a result, repeatedly deleting a minimum-weight cocircuit gives a $d$-approximation, and an optimal solution can be found deterministically in $n^{(2d-1)p+O(1)}$ time on $n$ elements. For graphs, $d=2$ and our framework specializes to the tree-packing approach. As applications, we bound the cogirth-strength ratio for two broad classes, and both bounds are tight. For quasi-graphic matroids, which include graphic, bicircular, frame, and lifted-graphic matroids, the ratio is at most $2$ for all weights, giving a $2$-approximation and an exact $n^{3p+O(1)}$-time algorithm. For $(k,\ell)$-count matroids of hypergraphs with $0\le \ell\le k$ and edge size at most $s$, the ratio is at most $ks$ under unit weights. This gives a $ks$-approximation and an exact $n^{(2ks-1)p+O(1)}$-time algorithm for unweighted rank-$p$ reduction.

papers.title: Architectures and KV Replay for Depth-Recurrent Language Models
papers.abstract: Depth recurrence increases effective model depth by repeatedly applying a fixed computation block. However, sharing attention parameters does not share the key-value (KV) states generated at different recurrence iterations, which causes memory growth with recurrence depth during autoregressive decoding. We study how to reduce this memory cost through architectural and cache-sharing approaches within a common depth-recurrent framework. We first study a looped hybrid that repeats a stack of Transformer layers, with recurrent mLSTM or Gated DeltaNet blocks replacing most attention layers and periodic Transformer attention anchors retained. We then restrict recurrence to a dedicated recurrent workspace in a Parcae-style architecture and test its stabilising adapter as a wrapper for the looped hybrid. Finally, we train a looped Transformer with recurrent KV replay, where only selected recurrence iterations write KV states that later iterations reuse. This trains the model to operate with the same shared KV topology used during inference. We find that looped hybrids require sufficiently frequent attention anchors, with performance depending strongly on the recurrent mixer. For cross-iteration KV sharing, recurrent KV replay allows multiple recurrence iterations to reuse the same KV states while retaining performance close to the full looped Transformer with separate KV caches for each iteration.

papers.title: PopulationBalanceModels.jl: An Extensible Framework for Deploying Population Balance Models
